flawed_step: 0031 (primary, on the main derivation path); also 0055
counterexample: Line 0031: with the proof's own inequality 2n <= 8(k-1)/(k-4), plug k=5: 8(k-1)/(k-4) = 8*4/1 = 32, not the '8 x 5 = 40' written. And the asserted comparison is numerically false either way: 32 > 2024 is false, and 40 > 2024 is false (2 x 1012 = 2024). So the sole stated justification for 'Thus k <= 4' is a false statement, and it is used in the wrong direction (RHS > 2n would be no contradiction at all; the contradiction actually needs RHS < 2n). Independent second counterexample, line 0055: the claimed equality condition 'every element appears in exactly 3 subsets' is refuted by the proof's own list in line 0059 -- element 1 lies in {1,2,3}, {1,3,4}, {1,4,5}, {1,5,6}, {1,6,2}, i.e. 5 subsets, not 3 (indeed 10 subsets x 3 elements / 6 elements = 5 incidences per element, and the correct condition is d_x = 2(2n-1)/(n-1) = 5).
reasoning_summary: The construction (lines 0005-0009) is fine: A,B of size floor(n/2), C,D of size ceil(n/2) partition [2n]; each of A u C, A u D, B u C, B u D has size n, and any three of them meet in the empty set (e.g. (AuC) n (AuD) = A, and A n (BuC) = empty). The counting frame (lines 0015-0029) is also fine: sum of column weights c_i equals kn over 2n columns, the convexified binomial in line 0070-0073 is genuinely convex so Jensen gives sum C(c_i,3) >= 2n*C(k/2,3), any three rows contribute at most one all-ones column triple so the total is at most C(k,3), and simplifying 2n*k(k-2)(k-4)/48 <= k(k-1)(k-2)/6 does yield 2n <= 8(k-1)/(k-4) for k >= 5. The failure is at line 0031, the single step that converts that inequality into the answer: the author computes the k=5 right-hand side as 8*5/1 (it is 8*4/1 = 32) and then asserts it exceeds 2 x 1012 = 2024, which is false for both 32 and 40; moreover, RHS > 2n is not a contradiction with 2n <= RHS, so the stated reasoning is backwards as well as arithmetically wrong. The correct contradiction is 2024 > 32, so the conclusion k <= 4 happens to be true, but the proof as written does not establish it. A second, unambiguous false claim appears at line 0055, where the derived equality condition for the n=3 bound is stated as 'every element appears in exactly 3 subsets'; the proof's own 10-subset example at line 0059 has every element in exactly 5 subsets (30 incidences over 6 elements), so this structural fact, which the reader is explicitly invited to use to build the construction, is wrong. Verified along the way that the pair condition in line 0057 is correct (all 15 pairs occur exactly twice in the line 0059 list), that k <= 4(2n-1)/(n-1) gives 10 at n=3, and that the OP argument in lines 0065-0066 is sound.
